narrative.note: Jordan, Riley is four and standing right at the starting line for so many exciting firsts, which is exactly where a curious four-year-old is meant to be.

subjects.math: Counting with real objects, one at a time, is the next skill on the horizon for Riley, and it's a hands-on one trucks make easy to practice.
subjects.literacy: Noticing that a sign or cereal box says something is the next step for Riley, an easy one to start pointing out together.
subjects.phonics: Clapping out the beats in a word, like ba-na-na, is next for Riley, and it's one of the most playful pre-reading skills to practice.
subjects.writing: Holding a crayon with fingers instead of a fist is the next step for Riley, one that tends to shift with more time drawing and coloring.
subjects.language: Telling you about something that happened earlier today is a big memory and language leap that's next for Riley.
subjects.science: Sorting things into groups, big versus small, animals versus plants, is the next thinking skill on Riley's list.
subjects.social_studies: Naming how family members connect, like knowing grandma is a parent's parent, is next for Riley to build through everyday conversation.
subjects.art: Naming the main colors while drawing or painting is the next step for Riley, one that grows with time at the easel.
subjects.music: Clapping or tapping along to a steady beat is next for Riley, and it's one of the easiest skills to turn into a game.
subjects.gross_motor: Galloping, with one foot leading the other, is the next big movement skill for Riley to try.
subjects.fine_motor: Stringing large beads or threading laces is next for Riley, building the hand strength that comes before writing.
subjects.social_emotional: Playing WITH other kids, taking turns and sharing with reminders, is the next social skill for Riley to grow into.
subjects.self_care: Using the toilet during the day, with just occasional misses, is the next step for Riley.
subjects.executive_function: Waiting a short turn without falling apart, even with support, is the next skill for Riley to build.
subjects.computer_science: This one is all about exposure, so whenever you and Riley want to play with step-by-step instructions, that's the perfect time to start.
subjects.spanish: This is about exposure too, so whenever it fits your family, understanding a few everyday words is a fun place to begin.

narrative.synthesis: Clapping the beats in a word and asking what a sign says are two pieces of the same reading foundation, so growth in one tends to support the other. Since reading is what you're most curious about, phonics could be a good place to lean in this month, playing sound games in the car or bath. There's no need to rush every subject at once; small, playful moments add up.

drawers.math: Touching each object while counting is what helps numbers click at this age. Counting trucks lined up in a row, going one higher each day, turns practice into a game.
drawers.literacy: Curiosity about print often starts small, with one sign or box catching their eye first. Pointing out letters on truck boxes or toy packaging is a low-key way to spark that noticing.
drawers.phonics: Hearing the beats in words like ba-na-na builds the ear that later hears individual sounds. A quick round of sound I-spy in the car or bath makes it easy to practice.
drawers.writing: A fist grip is common at this age and shifts naturally with more drawing time, not correction. Writing Riley's name big and letting them trace it in new colors turns practice into art.
drawers.language: Retelling what just happened asks a lot of memory and language at once, so it's normal to take a bit more time. Asking Riley to tell you what happened at the park hands over the story to practice.
drawers.science: Sorting by big and small or animal and plant is early thinking that grows through play, not worksheets. Sink or float with five small objects turns guessing into real science.
drawers.social_studies: Naming how family connects builds through repeated stories more than memorization. Drawing a simple map of home together and marking everyone's bed with a star is a fun, low-key way in.
drawers.art: Naming colors while creating grows through repeated exposure and modeling, not correction. Playing a song and drawing how it feels, fast scribbles for fast parts, builds that color vocabulary.
drawers.music: Keeping a steady beat grows through imitation games more than instruction. Clapping a short pattern and trading the leader role back and forth makes for an easy daily practice.
drawers.gross_motor: Galloping asks the body to coordinate two different leg jobs at once, so it often clicks a bit later than running or jumping. Animal races down the hallway, bear crawl, crab walk, frog jump, build that coordination through play.
drawers.fine_motor: Threading beads or laces builds the same hand strength that later makes writing easier. Snipping paper into confetti with child-safe scissors is a fun five-minute warm-up for that control.
drawers.social_emotional: Playing WITH other kids instead of near them grows through practice and reminders, not maturity alone. Naming the feeling first, then offering two choices, gives Riley a script for tricky moments.
drawers.self_care: Daytime toilet use with occasional misses is common at this age and tends to settle with consistent routines, not pressure. Turning independence tasks, like buttoning a shirt, into a timed game keeps things light.
drawers.executive_function: Waiting a turn without falling apart is one of the last self-control skills to solidify, since it asks a young brain to manage a strong feeling in real time. Freeze dance turns that waiting practice into a game Riley will ask for again.
drawers.computer_science: This skill is about exposure, not a timeline, so there's no rush here. Letting Riley program you across the room with exact steps, wrong turns included, makes debugging feel like a giggling game.
drawers.spanish: This one moves at whatever pace fits your family, with no age expectation attached. Picking one useful phrase and using it all week, at snack time or bedtime, helps it stick better than trying to cover many words at once.

narrative.keepsake:
Riley, right now you love trucks, lining them up just so, pushing them across the floor, making the engine sounds exactly right. Jordan watches you play and notices how carefully you look at every wheel and door before the race begins. You ask questions about everything around you, testing how things work, curious about the world one truck at a time. Jordan loves watching you grow into exactly who you are, one day at a time. Keep going, Riley.
